NSFAS fiasco

By: Sasha Schwendenwein | Commission

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
As we stand amidst the chaos gripping NSFAS, marked by the removal of Ernest Khosa and the dissolution of its board, coupled with students taking to the streets in protest (tragically leading to a stu

Unique Selling Point:
By using the narrative of the Ntumba brothers we will explain how corruption and mismanagement by board led to NSFAS's downfall, shedding light on their questionable dealings and revealing the systemic issues plaguing the organization.

Summary:
The narrative kicks off against the backdrop of the ongoing NSFAS saga: depending on how editorial wants to proceed: we could engage in a student interviews, encapsulate the unfolding news. It's essential to trace back its origins, recounting how NSFAS emerged as a hard-won victory during the 'fees must fall' movement. We'll revisit our past reports, where students passionately articulated their needs and aspirations. This journey illuminates how NSFAS evolved from a symbol of student resistance to a pivotal institution in higher education funding.

TREATMENT:
I have spoken to Mias and he has a lot of ideas of how we can achieve a dark, shadowy feel for the story. He is going to go through plug ins this weekend and also look at options for Peter to then copy on shoot. We have decided that we will have two different grades for the two brothers, and the feel will all depend on the lighting. He suggests Peter uses different colours for the lights to give each "brother" their own tint.
We will tastefully dramatize the brothers - and "hint" at the corrupt activities. I have sent them both Floris' story to show them what he did with the photos, and Mias says we can definitely do something like that.

Further information:
We would be introduced to how NSFAS has one job; to pay the nearly 1 million students so they can study. The Auditor General's revelation of a R177 million lease agreement that flouted procurement laws served as the final blow to Khosa's tenure. However, the seeds of this conflict were sown two years prior...

To streamline payment procedures, NSFAS forged partnerships with four companies, which profit from transaction fees when students utilize their NSFAS cards. However, these relationships have come under scrutiny for alleged corruption, yet no repercussions have been witnessed.

We will go into detail and context of who the Ntumba brothers are. Thulasizwe "Thula" Ntumba and Melusi Ntumba.
Thula: We'll show how Thulas wife's company benefitted by getting contracts because of their relationship with the NSFAS CEO.
Melusi's involvement extends beyond the NSFAS contracts; he has also been implicated in the Smart Billion fiasco. Approximately 580 clients entrusted funds to this company, only to discover that it traded their money without authorization and failed to reimburse the losses it incurred.

OUTA's Rudie Heyneke will explain the complexities of their investigation in the most straightforward manner. He’ll explain how the beneficiaries of the contracts stand to earn millions of rands.

Melusi's business ties with the former CEO of NSFAS, Andile Nongogo, date back to Nongogo's tenure as the CEO of SSETA. During this period, Thula's wife, Tsegofatso Ntumba, who serves as a director of Coinvest, a financial payment management company, received numerous tenders. Remarkably, this trend persisted even after Andile Nongogo transitioned to NSFAS as its CEO.

Fast forward to NSFAS: The company in question awarded the contract is Coinvest. Following Nongogo's departure, the portfolio committee advised the cancellation of these controversial "payment partner" contracts.
We'll delve into the recordings released on January 4th, 2024 (confirmed by Heyneke). These recordings unveil a tense exchange between CEO Earnest Khosa and Thula Ntumba, where Ntumba pleaded for their contracts to persist—a request that was ultimately granted. However, what heightens the intrigue is the revelation of a third individual in this conversation, whose identity remained unknown to OUTA at that time. This cliffhanger will tantalize audiences as we conclude Act 1, setting the stage for further revelations and unravelling of the NSFAS saga.

With regards to Melusi Ntumba: We will speak with case study Petrus Mokoena and his lawyer Cwayita Kalenga:

Smart Billion traded in contracts for differences on behalf of clients through an online trading platform, GT247. Smart Billion opened a trading account at GT247, pooled client funds, and traded it in the name of Smart Billion. Clients deposited funds for trading purposes into Smart Billion's bank account, but only "a miniscule amount" was transferred to GT247 for trading purposes. The balance of the client funds that remained in Smart Billion's bank account was used to pay clients' withdrawal requests, as well as personal and business expenses.
The FSCA came down hard on Smart Billion, and Melusi was given an administrative penalty of R10 million he was debarred him for a period of 10 years.
According to FSCA; “Ntumba, in his capacity as director and CEO of Smart Billion, did not observe the utmost good faith and did not exercise proper care and diligence with regards to client funds.” Criminal charges have been laid against Ntumba.

But now we have something new that no one else has – Melusi Ntumba is continuing to operate his accounting firm in Sandton despite being in breach of SAICA rules adds a new layer of intrigue to the story. As a member of SAICA, his alleged misconduct raises questions about his fitness to handle financial matters. While we'll seek an interview with SAICA for their perspective, the lawyer involved will also shed light on this matter, further deepening our exploration of Ntumba's controversial activities.

Confront of Melusi and Thula Ntumba
Ask NSFAS and minister Blade for interviews
ROR: Former CEOs Nongogo and Khosa
The plot thickens as OUTA reveals the identity of the mysterious third man in the audio recording: businessman Joshua Maluleke. Maluleke's associations raise eyebrows, as he is a member of the board of directors of the OR Tambo School of Leadership, closely linked to the ANC. Furthermore, he is a co-director of Zipsilor, a company implicated in corrupt activities related to designated for a rehabilitation centre in Soshanguve. Maluleke's connections extend to President Ramaphosa's brother, Douglas Ramaphosa, with whom he shares business ventures and serves alongside at the OR Tambo School of Leadership. This revelation adds yet another layer of complexity to the unfolding NSFAS saga, hinting at deeper political and business entanglements.
We will ask all sorts of questions about this and we’ll call Maluleke. And end with the final conclusions remember that while students are desperate to study, NSFAS is in tatters… A situation that isn’t going to be resolved in the next few weeks…


Confront of Melusi and Thula Ntumba and Thula's wife
Ask NSFAS and minister Blade for interviews
ROR: Former CEOs Nongogo and Khosa

1. The case study is in Bloemfontein
2. We need to potentially buy some news footage

Script:






UPS: “Our enemy is the ANC, not OUTA” (paraphrasing)



VO: A leaked recording of a conversation that shouldn’t have happened. (PAUSE) And its significance lies not only in what’s being said but also… who’s saying it.



Broll: Govan listening



VO: It reveals worrying governance issues at an organisation looking after the financial needs of students as well as apparent proximity to power stretching all the way to Cabinet.



UPS: “The pressure will seize on us and on the Minister.”



FTB



UPS OUT: “…from poor and working-class backgrounds (applause).”



VO: An announcement by President Zuma celebrated by the 2016 Fees Must Fall movement. It caught many in his own party by surprise.





GOVAN: Zuma’s announcement flew in the face of a conclusion reached by a committee he himself had established to investigate the fees issue.  The commission found it was unaffordable - but Zuma pushed ahead, adding a new and significant line to the budget.





VO: In 2018, the National Student Financial Aid Scheme, or NSFAS, was re-launched to include free tertiary education for students from households earning less than R350,000 a year. Since then, over R120 billion has been spent on nearly 3 million students. 







This story is about two government agencies, a private company, and a civil society watchdog. It has five main characters and is set in the dramatic unravelling of NSFAS in the years following its relaunch. (PAUSE) It’s also about a damning forensic investigation – which is where the story begins.



UPS: Start of studio link and slowly fade..



VO: Late last year an investigation by the law firm, Werksman’s pointed to irregularities in the appointment of so-called “Direct Payment Service Providers” at NSFAS. These are private companies awarded tenders to make payments to students.



To understand their role in this story, it’s necessary to meet the first of our five characters.




UPS: (02:24) “We fund people so they can change their own circumstances, the circumstances of their families and their communities .”



VO: Andile Nongogo was appointed CEO of NSFAS in late 2020. He was fired just three years later after Werksman’s found he’d interfered in the appointment of the Payment Service Providers.



PAUSE



But Nongogo still casts a shadow over NSFAS, as do three other key characters.





UPS: From the promo vid



VO: Businesswoman, Tshegofatso Ntumba, is married to this man: Thulasizwe or Thula. His brother is Melusi Ntumba, an accountant whose firm is STILL on the panel of internal auditors at NSFAS despite him being implicated in a Ponzi scheme and facing a criminal trial.



Tshegofatso is a director of a company called Coinvest Africa. Remember the name:



It's claimed Thula Ntumba is the real powerbroker behind Coinvest.

PAUSE



To explain our focus on the Ntumbas over the other parties implicated in the Werksman’s report, we need to go back in time.

VO: Prior to joining NSFAS, Nongogo was the Chief Executive of what’s known as the Services SETA, a Sector Education and Training Agency. And among the personalities it did business with were the Ntumbas.

Rudie Heyneke:Tshegofatso Ntumba was a director at a company, they received a branding tender to the tune of almost 29 million rand.

VO: Rudi Heyneke is from the civil society watchdog, OUTA. He’s been on the Nongogo/Ntumba trail for some time, and says in the SETA years, their relationship flourished.

Rudie Heyneke: He paid one of the Ntumba brothers an amount of 40,000 rand. What it showed us is that there was a relationship.  (Note joined UPS) We also saw that Ntumba Associates and consulting, they got a lot of tenders 







VO: So, We have a government agency known as a SETA headed by Nongogo – an official who would later become the focus of the Werksmans investigation. And we have the Ntumba’s – three characters key to understanding our story – two of whom are linked to a company called Coinvest.

So that’s our trip back in time concluded. Back to the current controversy.



UPS: Naledi Pandor @ 10:12 “We will continue to ensure that the funding that our young people should have, gets to them and supports them to succeed academically.”



VO: A 2018 speech by then Minister of Higher Education, Naledi Pandor, as NSFAS was still grappling with its new financial challenges. It would be another two years before Nongogo’s appointment as CEO.

PAUSE

And with his arrival came a new way of getting money into students’ pockets.



Rudie: Previous tenders that went out from NSFAS said that the service provider must pay the student directly to his bank account and now this changed they developed the NSFAS bank card.

Every month, the nearly one million NSFAS bursary students each receive a monthly allowance. In 2022, four “Payment Service Providers” were enlisted to manage those payments via ‘NSFAS cards’

And here, one of the circles in our story closes: One of those companies was none other than Coinvest.

Rudie: none of them were. you know. Experienced. There's a lot of high uh service fees that the students are charged with. 

Students were charged transaction fees of around R70 per month by The Payment Service Providers - exceeding what a commercial bank would charge for almost every service.



Pause

It could be argued that the fees structure discourages unnecessary spending, but it’s clear the Payment Service Providers – among them, Coinvest - were making good money.

Pause

But, after Werksman’s published its investigation, the entire lucrative enterprise came crashing down.

















VO: Nongogo was fired and Werksman’s recommended that the contracts with the four payment service providers be cancelled.

So you’ve met four of our main characters, but we promised you five. (Brief pause) And here is where we reveal why Coinvest is getting all our attention.



UPS: “Let’s say we investigate Andile… (break into two using Govan as cutaway)

Earlier this year, OUTA published two leaked audio recordings of conversations that took place in August last year. In them, three men are heard discussing the then-incomplete Werksmans investigation and how it might impact them.

UPS “I know all the things we did together in the corners, and I know where we can be caught.”

VO: One of the voices belongs to our story’s fifth and final character, at the time the chair of the NSFAS board, Ernest Khosa.

Pause

The identities of the other two men have been less widely publicised, but one is none other than Thula Ntumba. Even though his wife, Tshegofatso, is the Coinvest director, Khosa clearly considers Thula the de facto owner.

UPS: “The pressure will seize on us, and on the Minister”

Rudie: Mister Khosa gave these two gentlemen in a thorough and detailed feedback on what is happening and what they've decided to do

Govan: He's briefing an implicated party, almost?

Rudie: a chairperson of a board should not meet with a service provider. The question is um did Mister Khosa report back to the board?

VO: The answer, later confirmed by NSFAS in a statement, is that no, he didn’t. 

Rudie: They asked for an extension for the contracts. There was no talk about anything about students, their problems and their issues. 

VO: It had been Khosa who’d announced Nongogo’s firing, accusing him of:

Failing to act “honestly, faithfully and diligently…”

Failing to “…promote and protect the best interests of NSFAS.”

And of “…breaching the trust relationship” between himself and NSFAS”

Pause

VO: And yet this entire saga came from Nongogo’s alleged influence in the appointment of the Payment Service Providers – one of whom Khosa was now accused of having a highly irregular meeting with. Also concerning, is the apparently tight relationship between Khosa and Higher Education Minister, Blade Nzimande.



VO: Khosa would later resign as board chairman but, for Thula, the meeting appears to have paid off.

UPSOUND: recording 2 at 09:38

Mr C: "But if we can push for three months and plan the end game properly instead of saying we want to take out Coinvest, we want to take out all of you…"



Pause

The Werksman’s report recommended that the four Payment Service Provider contracts be cancelled – something the board committed to doing. But eight months later, that hadn’t happened.

NSFAS call to Ishmael Mnisi: 

Govan: We would like to know when NSFAS is going to cancel the Coinvest contract? 

VO: Last month, we asked NSFAS spokesperson, Ishmael Mnisi why not.

Mnisi: The board said they’re going to implement all the very recommendations which includes the termination of this contract

Govan: Can you tell us why it's taken so long to take legal advice on the cancellation of the contract? 

Mnisi: You can't just cancel a contract without er er taking it through the the legal eh process. 

Nongogo, Khosa and Minister Nzimande didn’t respond to questions. Khosa has taken OUTA to court, insisting they withdraw their reports. 

On whether he’s running Coinvest on his wife’s behalf, Thula didn’t respond; nor did he indicate whether he negotiated an extension of its NSFAS contract.

Melusi denied having anything to do with Coinvest or Thula’s dealings and said he couldn’t comment on the Ponzi scheme allegations as he’s testifying in the liquidations process.

Tshegofatso denied that she has a relationship with Nongogo and said allegations against Coinvest are untrue.

And so, our story comes to an end: Two state agencies, a private company, a civil society watchdog, and five main characters. And let’s not forget the tens of thousands of students who are the real victims of this mess.

VO: Late last year an investigation by the law firm, Werksman’s pointed to irregularities in the appointment of so-called “Direct Payment Service Providers” at NSFAS. These are private companies awarded tenders to make payments to students. To understand their role in this story, it’s necessary to meet the first of our five characters. UPS: (02:24) “We fund people so they can change their own circumstances, the circumstances of their families and their communities .” VO: Andile Nongogo was appointed CEO of NSFAS in late 2020. He was fired just three years later after Werksman’s found he’d interfered in the appointment of the Payment Service Providers. PAUSE But Nongogo still casts a shadow over NSFAS, as do three other key characters. UPS: From the promo vid VO: Businesswoman, Tshegofatso Ntumba, is married to this man: Thulasizwe or Thula. His brother is Melusi Ntumba, an accountant whose firm is STILL on the panel of internal auditors at NSFAS despite him being implicated in a Ponzi scheme and facing a criminal trial. Tshegofatso is a director of a company called Coinvest Africa. Remember the name: It's claimed Thula Ntumba is the real powerbroker behind Coinvest. PAUSE To explain our focus on the Ntumbas over the other parties implicated in the Werksman’s report, we need to go back in time. VO: Prior to joining NSFAS, Nongogo was the Chief Executive of what’s known as the Services SETA, a Sector Education and Training Agency. And among the personalities it did business with were the Ntumbas. Rudie Heyneke:Tshegofatso Ntumba was a director at a company, they received a branding tender to the tune of almost 29 million rand. VO: Rudi Heyneke is from the civil society watchdog, OUTA. He’s been on the Nongogo/Ntumba trail for some time, and says in the SETA years, their relationship flourished. Rudie Heyneke: He paid one of the Ntumba brothers an amount of 40,000 rand. What it showed us is that there was a relationship. (Note joined UPS) We also saw that Ntumba Associates and consulting, they got a lot of tenders VO: So, We have a government agency known as a SETA headed by Nongogo – an official who would later become the focus of the Werksmans investigation. And we have the Ntumba’s – three characters key to understanding our story – two of whom are linked to a company called Coinvest. So that’s our trip back in time concluded. Back to the current controversy. UPS: Naledi Pandor @ 10:12 “We will continue to ensure that the funding that our young people should have, gets to them and supports them to succeed academically.” VO: A 2018 speech by then Minister of Higher Education, Naledi Pandor, as NSFAS was still grappling with its new financial challenges. It would be another two years before Nongogo’s appointment as CEO. PAUSE And with his arrival came a new way of getting money into students’ pockets. Rudie: Previous tenders that went out from NSFAS said that the service provider must pay the student directly to his bank account and now this changed they developed the NSFAS bank card. Every month, the nearly one million NSFAS bursary students each receive a monthly allowance. In 2022, four “Payment Service Providers” were enlisted to manage those payments via ‘NSFAS cards’ And here, one of the circles in our story closes: One of those companies was none other than Coinvest. Rudie: none of them were. you know. Experienced. There's a lot of high uh service fees that the students are charged with. Students were charged transaction fees of around R70 per month by The Payment Service Providers - exceeding what a commercial bank would charge for almost every service. Pause It could be argued that the fees structure discourages unnecessary spending, but it’s clear the Payment Service Providers – among them, Coinvest - were making good money. Pause But, after Werksman’s published its investigation, the entire lucrative enterprise came crashing down. VO: Nongogo was fired and Werksman’s recommended that the contracts with the four payment service providers be cancelled. So you’ve met four of our main characters, but we promised you five. (Brief pause) And here is where we reveal why Coinvest is getting all our attention. UPS: “Let’s say we investigate Andile… (break into two using Govan as cutaway) Earlier this year, OUTA published two leaked audio recordings of conversations that took place in August last year. In them, three men are heard discussing the then-incomplete Werksmans investigation and how it might impact them. UPS “I know all the things we did together in the corners, and I know where we can be caught.” VO: One of the voices belongs to our story’s fifth and final character, at the time the chair of the NSFAS board, Ernest Khosa. Pause The identities of the other two men have been less widely publicised, but one is none other than Thula Ntumba. Even though his wife, Tshegofatso, is the Coinvest director, Khosa clearly considers Thula the de facto owner. UPS: “The pressure will seize on us, and on the Minister” Rudie: Mister Khosa gave these two gentlemen in a thorough and detailed feedback on what is happening and what they've decided to do Govan: He's briefing an implicated party, almost? Rudie: a chairperson of a board should not meet with a service provider. The question is um did Mister Khosa report back to the board? VO: The answer, later confirmed by NSFAS in a statement, is that no, he didn’t. Rudie: They asked for an extension for the contracts. There was no talk about anything about students, their problems and their issues. VO: It had been Khosa who’d announced Nongogo’s firing, accusing him of: Failing to act “honestly, faithfully and diligently…” Failing to “…promote and protect the best interests of NSFAS.” And of “…breaching the trust relationship” between himself and NSFAS” Pause VO: And yet this entire saga came from Nongogo’s alleged influence in the appointment of the Payment Service Providers – one of whom Khosa was now accused of having a highly irregular meeting with. Also concerning, is the apparently tight relationship between Khosa and Higher Education Minister, Blade Nzimande. VO: Khosa would later resign as board chairman but, for Thula, the meeting appears to have paid off. UPSOUND: recording 2 at 09:38 Mr C: "But if we can push for three months and plan the end game properly instead of saying we want to take out Coinvest, we want to take out all of you…" Pause The Werksman’s report recommended that the four Payment Service Provider contracts be cancelled – something the board committed to doing. But eight months later, that hadn’t happened. NSFAS call to Ishmael Mnisi: Govan: We would like to know when NSFAS is going to cancel the Coinvest contract? VO: Last month, we asked NSFAS spokesperson, Ishmael Mnisi why not. Mnisi: The board said they’re going to implement all the very recommendations which includes the termination of this contract Govan: Can you tell us why it's taken so long to take legal advice on the cancellation of the contract? Mnisi: You can't just cancel a contract without er er taking it through the the legal eh process. Nongogo, Khosa and Minister Nzimande didn’t respond to questions. Khosa has taken OUTA to court, insisting they withdraw their reports. On whether he’s running Coinvest on his wife’s behalf, Thula didn’t respond; nor did he indicate whether he negotiated an extension of its NSFAS contract. Melusi denied having anything to do with Coinvest or Thula’s dealings and said he couldn’t comment on the Ponzi scheme allegations as he’s testifying in the liquidations process. Tshegofatso denied that she has a relationship with Nongogo and said allegations against Coinvest are untrue. And so, our story comes to an end: Two state agencies, a private company, a civil society watchdog, and five main characters. And let’s not forget the tens of thousands of students who are the real victims of this mess.

metadata.Unique Selling Point: By using the narrative of the Ntumba brothers we will explain how corruption and mismanagement by board led to NSFAS's downfall, shedding light on their questionable dealings and revealing the systemic issues plaguing the organization.
metadata.Summary: The narrative kicks off against the backdrop of the ongoing NSFAS saga: depending on how editorial wants to proceed: we could engage in a student interviews, encapsulate the unfolding news. It's essential to trace back its origins, recounting how NSFAS emerged as a hard-won victory during the 'fees must fall' movement. We'll revisit our past reports, where students passionately articulated their needs and aspirations. This journey illuminates how NSFAS evolved from a symbol of student resistance to a pivotal institution in higher education funding. TREATMENT: I have spoken to Mias and he has a lot of ideas of how we can achieve a dark, shadowy feel for the story. He is going to go through plug ins this weekend and also look at options for Peter to then copy on shoot. We have decided that we will have two different grades for the two brothers, and the feel will all depend on the lighting. He suggests Peter uses different colours for the lights to give each "brother" their own tint. We will tastefully dramatize the brothers - and "hint" at the corrupt activities. I have sent them both Floris' story to show them what he did with the photos, and Mias says we can definitely do something like that.
metadata.Further information: We would be introduced to how NSFAS has one job; to pay the nearly 1 million students so they can study. The Auditor General's revelation of a R177 million lease agreement that flouted procurement laws served as the final blow to Khosa's tenure. However, the seeds of this conflict were sown two years prior... To streamline payment procedures, NSFAS forged partnerships with four companies, which profit from transaction fees when students utilize their NSFAS cards. However, these relationships have come under scrutiny for alleged corruption, yet no repercussions have been witnessed. We will go into detail and context of who the Ntumba brothers are. Thulasizwe "Thula" Ntumba and Melusi Ntumba. Thula: We'll show how Thulas wife's company benefitted by getting contracts because of their relationship with the NSFAS CEO. Melusi's involvement extends beyond the NSFAS contracts; he has also been implicated in the Smart Billion fiasco. Approximately 580 clients entrusted funds to this company, only to discover that it traded their money without authorization and failed to reimburse the losses it incurred. OUTA's Rudie Heyneke will explain the complexities of their investigation in the most straightforward manner. He’ll explain how the beneficiaries of the contracts stand to earn millions of rands. Melusi's business ties with the former CEO of NSFAS, Andile Nongogo, date back to Nongogo's tenure as the CEO of SSETA. During this period, Thula's wife, Tsegofatso Ntumba, who serves as a director of Coinvest, a financial payment management company, received numerous tenders. Remarkably, this trend persisted even after Andile Nongogo transitioned to NSFAS as its CEO. Fast forward to NSFAS: The company in question awarded the contract is Coinvest. Following Nongogo's departure, the portfolio committee advised the cancellation of these controversial "payment partner" contracts. We'll delve into the recordings released on January 4th, 2024 (confirmed by Heyneke). These recordings unveil a tense exchange between CEO Earnest Khosa and Thula Ntumba, where Ntumba pleaded for their contracts to persist—a request that was ultimately granted. However, what heightens the intrigue is the revelation of a third individual in this conversation, whose identity remained unknown to OUTA at that time. This cliffhanger will tantalize audiences as we conclude Act 1, setting the stage for further revelations and unravelling of the NSFAS saga. With regards to Melusi Ntumba: We will speak with case study Petrus Mokoena and his lawyer Cwayita Kalenga: Smart Billion traded in contracts for differences on behalf of clients through an online trading platform, GT247. Smart Billion opened a trading account at GT247, pooled client funds, and traded it in the name of Smart Billion. Clients deposited funds for trading purposes into Smart Billion's bank account, but only "a miniscule amount" was transferred to GT247 for trading purposes. The balance of the client funds that remained in Smart Billion's bank account was used to pay clients' withdrawal requests, as well as personal and business expenses. The FSCA came down hard on Smart Billion, and Melusi was given an administrative penalty of R10 million he was debarred him for a period of 10 years. According to FSCA; “Ntumba, in his capacity as director and CEO of Smart Billion, did not observe the utmost good faith and did not exercise proper care and diligence with regards to client funds.” Criminal charges have been laid against Ntumba. But now we have something new that no one else has – Melusi Ntumba is continuing to operate his accounting firm in Sandton despite being in breach of SAICA rules adds a new layer of intrigue to the story. As a member of SAICA, his alleged misconduct raises questions about his fitness to handle financial matters. While we'll seek an interview with SAICA for their perspective, the lawyer involved will also shed light on this matter, further deepening our exploration of Ntumba's controversial activities. Confront of Melusi and Thula Ntumba Ask NSFAS and minister Blade for interviews ROR: Former CEOs Nongogo and Khosa The plot thickens as OUTA reveals the identity of the mysterious third man in the audio recording: businessman Joshua Maluleke. Maluleke's associations raise eyebrows, as he is a member of the board of directors of the OR Tambo School of Leadership, closely linked to the ANC. Furthermore, he is a co-director of Zipsilor, a company implicated in corrupt activities related to designated for a rehabilitation centre in Soshanguve. Maluleke's connections extend to President Ramaphosa's brother, Douglas Ramaphosa, with whom he shares business ventures and serves alongside at the OR Tambo School of Leadership. This revelation adds yet another layer of complexity to the unfolding NSFAS saga, hinting at deeper political and business entanglements. We will ask all sorts of questions about this and we’ll call Maluleke. And end with the final conclusions remember that while students are desperate to study, NSFAS is in tatters… A situation that isn’t going to be resolved in the next few weeks… Confront of Melusi and Thula Ntumba and Thula's wife Ask NSFAS and minister Blade for interviews ROR: Former CEOs Nongogo and Khosa
